answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: American author, motivational speaker & comedian · nearest documented source
answer.sourceLine: C.S. Lewis never wrote this line — it appears in none of his books, and both the C.S. Lewis Foundation and Christianity Today list it as misattributed. The closest documented wording is in Charles Marshall’s 2003 book Shattering the Glass Slipper, but the exact popular phrasing is an anonymous modern paraphrase of an older “character is what you do when no one is watching” maxim, so no single originator can be pinned to it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Misattributed — modern paraphrase, no single originator

source.excerpt: Integrity is doing the right thing when you don’t have to — when no one else is looking or will ever know — when there will be no congratulations or recognition for having done so.
trail: The C.S. Lewis Foundation lists the line among quotes misattributed to Lewis, calling it a paraphrase of a Charles Marshall quote in Shattering the Glass Slipper.
Christianity Today’s survey of the top misquoted Lewis lines confirms the phrase is absent from his work and traces the closest wording to Marshall’s 2003 book.
Teacher Sam Young’s multi-year investigation searched Mere Christianity and found no such sentence, and could locate no primary Lewis source.
A related older maxim — “Character is doing what’s right when nobody’s looking” — is documented for J.C. Watts in the 1990s per Young’s follow-up, showing the idea predates any “integrity” wording.
source.excerptNote: The nearest documented wording, from Charles Marshall’s Shattering the Glass Slipper (2003), as quoted by Christianity Today. Marshall presents it as his own words, not as a Lewis quotation — and it differs from the smoothed-out popular version.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase that cannot be tied to a single dated first publication, so no copyright status is asserted. The nearest documented phrasing — Charles Marshall’s Shattering the Glass Slipper (2003) — would itself be in-copyright to Marshall/his publisher, but it is a different sentence, not the line as usually quoted.

author.name: Charles Marshall
author.heading: About Charles Marshall
author.bio: Charles W. Marshall is an American motivational speaker, comedian and author who addresses corporate and civic audiences across the United States. His 2003 book Shattering the Glass Slipper contains the sentence most often cited as the source of this quotation — written in his own voice, with no reference to C.S. Lewis. Even so, his phrasing differs from the tidy popular version, and the underlying idea long predates him.

misattribution.heading: How C.S. Lewis got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reshared lines pinned on C.S. Lewis — but it is a classic “magnet-name” misattribution: a tidy, quotable maxim attached to a beloved author who never wrote it.

items.why: The line appears in none of Lewis’s books, and is frequently but wrongly cited to Mere Christianity (1952). The C.S. Lewis Foundation and Christianity Today both list it as misattributed.

His 2003 Shattering the Glass Slipper contains “Integrity is doing the right thing when you don’t have to…” in his own voice — but this is a fuller, different sentence, so it is the closest documented match, not proof he coined the popular one-liner.

The near-identical “Character is doing what’s right when nobody’s looking” is documented for J.C. Watts in the 1990s per Sam Young’s research, showing the sentiment circulated widely before any “integrity” version.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: C.S. Lewis did not write this. The nearest documented wording is Charles Marshall’s 2003 book, and the exact popular phrasing is an anonymous modern paraphrase of a much older maxim.

context.heading: Why the attribution sticks
lead: Lewis is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good, morally tidy lines — his real reputation for writing plainly about virtue makes almost any aphorism about character sound like something he could have said. Once a quote-card pairs the sentence with his name, it self-replicates.

In reality the “do right when unobserved” idea is an old and widely shared one, expressed by many writers about both character and integrity. The specific “Integrity is doing the right thing, even when no one is watching” wording is a smoothed, anonymous version whose earliest exact appearance no researcher has pinned down.
context.pull: Lewis never wrote it — it just sounds like he might have.
